newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani opposition confident will win polls.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani opposition confident will win polls.

text.p: Pakistani opposition leader Nawaz Sharif said on Tuesday the sacking of Benazir Bhutto's government was "deliverance for the people", and expressed confidence he would win general elections set for February.

"This day today is a day of deliverance for the people of Pakistan. The mismanagement of this government, the mishandling of this government is itself responsible for the situation which has arisen today," Sharif told Reuters after addressing supporters.

Asked if he was confident his Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party would win general polls which President Farooq Leghari set for next February 3, Sharif said: "So far, yes, we are. Not only confident, but very confident, God willing."
Surrounded by a crowd of party workers, Sharif said Leghari had adhered to the constitution in dissolving the lower house of parliament and sacking Bhutto's government.
"We did not want any extra-constitutional action in this country," he said.

"I think the government should really have realised what it was up to, what it is doing, and should have tried to avoid the situation. I think it is the government which is responsible for inviting the situation."
Earlier, in an Islamic gesture of thanksgiving, joyous PML activists slit the throat of a goat outside party headquarters.
Sharif was asked if the judiciary should prosecute members of the ousted government.
"I do not recommend any out-of-the-way actions against anybody, against any member of the opposition or against any member of the ousted party," he said. "I think the law should take its own course."

In his proclamation ousting Bhutto, the president accused her government of corruption and nepotism. Soldiers in the Punjab provincial capital of Lahore detained Bhutto's husband Asif Ali Zardari. There was no immediate explanation, but Zardari has been at the centre of corruption allegations.
Earlier, PML secretary-general Sartaj Aziz praised the president's action in appointing veteran politician Meraj Khalid, 80, as caretaker prime minister to supervise elections.
"We welcome the decision and welcome the appointment of Meraj Khalid," Aziz told Reuters by telephone, describing him as a "neutral, patriotic person".
He said the prospect that elections would be held in 90 days' time augured well for democracy and the political process.
Aziz urged the caretaker government to set up a system to bring people involved in corruption to justice and not wait for elections. "It should be a bi-partisan and credible system," he said.
